summary: An April 1 satirical proposal for a Firewall Enhancement Protocol that would let new technologies pass through firewalls without breaking their security model. It is a joke and not a real protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st satire proposes carrying network packets inside ordinary HTTP messages. The joke is that the method would let applications pass through a firewall that allows HTTP.

subtitle: An April 1st satire that wraps TCP/IP packets inside HTTP messages to cross firewalls.

tldr.problem: This April 1st joke satirizes the tension between firewalls and experimentation with new applications.
tldr.mechanism: It proposes carrying IP datagrams in HTTP message bodies and encoding TCP fields in HTTP headers.
tldr.outcome: FEP is a satirical proposal, not an endorsed way to bypass a firewall or an Internet standard.

facts.label: HTTP port named in the memo

today: RFC 3093 is an Informational April 1st satire about tunneling traffic through firewalls.

sections.title: Firewalls and the End-to-End Idea
sections.content:
The memo argues that firewalls can make it harder for people inside an organization to experiment with new applications. It proposes the Firewall Enhancement Protocol (FEP) as a way to carry application traffic through a firewall using HTTP.

The RFC says FEP requires an application inside the firewall that can access TCP port 80. Its claims about security and bypassing administrators are part of the April 1st satire.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC jokes that HTTP can carry other network traffic through a firewall. It frames this as restoring experimentation while avoiding firewall changes.

sections.title: Encapsulating Packets in HTTP
sections.content:
In the described flow, FEP software receives a TCP/IP datagram, places it in an HTTP message, and sends it through a tunnel to another host. The receiving FEP software decodes the message and passes the datagram into the destination host's protocol stack.

The IP datagram is encoded in the HTTP message body. TCP header fields, and optionally IP header fields, are also represented as readable HTTP headers.
sections.plainLanguage: One FEP program puts a network packet into an HTTP message. Another FEP program removes it and passes the packet to its application.

sections.title: The Satirical Security Claim
sections.content:
The RFC argues that the firewall still protects against outside threats because FEP requires cooperation from a host inside the firewall. It describes FEP traffic as using the ordinary HTTP port, while claiming the approach does not violate the firewall's security model.

It also jokes that users could choose applications without an administrator's approval and that readable headers could make tools such as tcpdump obsolete. The document is an April 1st satire, not operational security advice.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke rests on the claim that wrapping traffic in HTTP keeps the firewall intact while bypassing its restrictions. This is satire, not guidance for real network security.
